#4766. Mayan chieftain named ‘Bat’ ruled over an isolated jungle city

Published Nov 10, 2026 2:33 PM EST

Violent disputes between neighbors and a king named “Bat.” These and other new details about a recently rediscovered, ancient Maya city located in the remote tropical forests of southeast Mexico are beginning to come to light. The approximately 37-acre settlement is so inaccessible that archaeologists initially nicknamed the site Minanbé, or “there is no road” in Yucatec Maya. Despite a challenging journey to the site, researchers have identified multiple building remnants dating back at least 1,100 years. Historical records also indicate heated regional conflicts, and even a local chieftain’s animal-inspired name.

The Mayan Late Classic community was only discovered in May 2026 in the Mexican state Campeche, which shares its southern border with Guatemala. Subsequent hieroglyphic translations from National Autonomous University of Mexico archaeologist Octavio Esparza Olguín, suggest the city’s residents called their settlement Sakil, a Maya term relating to “whiteness.”

Located north of the Calakmul Biosphere Reserve, Minanbé’s surviving structures include religious facilities, palace structures, plazas, water-management systems, and even a nearly 43-foot-tall pyramid. However, archaeologists identified more than architectural features here. After examining 14 pillars and altars, researchers uncovered hieroglyphic records of a violent conflict between Sakil and a rival Mayan hub, Ocomtún. One particular monument’s carved relief depicts a captive lying on his stomach with his wrists tied and head turned sideways. Nearby inscriptions explain the individual was once a resident of Minanbé.

Hieroglyphics on other pillars memorialize a specific regional ruler (kalo’mte’) named Suutz’, which means “bat” in Yucatec Maya. Associated imagery depicts a ruler wearing decorative clothing, sandals, and a detailed headdress. Combined with additional signage, Esparza Olguín and his colleagues believe Suutz’ was a powerful chief who wielded a large amount of authority over Sakil’s residents.

Although the latest archaeological discoveries imply some type of military conflict between Sakil and Ocomtún, it’s still unclear if the problems occurred during the Suutz’ reign. Still, the recent excavations have revealed a great deal in a short amount of time. With more work, the team hopes to learn more about the recently rediscovered settlement, and its residents’ relationship to the world around them.

#4765. Finding Solace and Comfort in Listening to Trees

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

As we approach the holiday season, each of us needs to find ways to take time for ourselves to recover from the activities and responsibilities of the season. Attention restoration theory, proposed by Kaplan and Kaplan (1989), suggests that if we are able to spend time in natural spaces, we can feel rested, renewed, and better able to cope with the stressors and demands of the season. Listening to trees is one healing practice that offers such a possibility by calming the mind and body. Through this practice, we can develop a deeper understanding of ourselves, where we are in life, how we feel, what is important to us, and what we need during this season.

Listening to trees is one contemplative, meditative practice that invites us to slow down, become more attentive, and be more fully present in our everyday lives. At the same time, spending quiet, contemplative time in natural spaces can lead us to experience feelings of transcendence. Transcendent experiences deepen our sense of connection to ourselves, to the natural world, to other people, and to something larger than our individual lives.

Each person experiences transcendence differently. For some, it is connected to religious beliefs and spiritual practices; for others, it emerges through mind-body practice; for others, creative engagement can lead to transcendence. Experiencing transcendence does not involve the withdrawal from the trials and tribulations of everyday life. Instead, it helps us to be more deeply engaged with life by opening ourselves to a greater sense of connection, meaning, and belonging. Transcendent experiences serve dual purposes. They help us not only to ground ourselves more fully in the moment but also to connect to something that surpasses the immediate moment.

The theory of transcendence (Tornstam, 1977) suggests that as we age, we tend to shift our perspective toward more spiritual and cosmic concerns. According to this view, transcendence includes a shift in meaning by recognizing that time is limited, and understanding and accepting the past while at the same time being more fully in the present. It also includes integrating and accepting all aspects of the self, and placing greater emphasis on connections and relationships (social transcendence), and the well-being of the planet. Transcendence in later life, or gerotranscendence, encompasses all three dimensions and focuses on a deep connection with the natural flow of life, with natural spaces, with the future of the planet, and future generations. As we acknowledge that our time is limited, transcendence can help us heal from loss, cope with bereavement, and navigate day-to-day expectations. Transcendence prompts us to shift our focus more fully to what truly matters, while at the same time connecting us to something beyond our individual lives.

One therapeutic way of promoting transcendence is to regularly engage with nature — to listen to trees. Natural spaces provide solace, comfort, and healing, particularly in later life as aging adults contemplate the world they will leave behind. We also know that our individual well-being and happiness are intricately connected to the well-being of the planet. Listening to trees, walking through forests, spending time in parks and on beaches, or simply viewing nature are all physically and psychologically restorative and healing. The Biophilia Hypothesis (Wilson, 1984) even suggests that our connection with nature and natural spaces is fundamental to our survival. Natural immersion, even a few minutes daily in natural spaces, can also deepen our sensory awareness and draw our attention beyond our worries and anxieties toward a transcendent view in which we reflect on who we are, our place in the world, and what will be left when we are no longer here.

Certainly, human beings are not able to survive if nature does not. Our connection to nature is deeply rooted in our biology. Consciously or unconsciously, we have psychological, emotional, and physical connections to the natural world. I first learned about biophilia, our innate human tendency to be connected to nature and living organisms, in graduate school, when I studied the work of psychologist Erich Fromm. Fromm used the term in relation to a love of life and all that is alive (Fromm, 1973). This view has continued to inform my work and my personal life. In my ongoing work on well-being in later life, it has often been evident that our relationship with nature can sustain us throughout our lives, particularly during periods of vulnerability and loss.

In a culture of haste, in our busy lives, and particularly during the winter holidays, when the days are short and light is limited, burnout is an ever-present possibility. Psychological theories have suggested that if we can find the time to connect with natural spaces during this time, we can manage our stressors and demands more effectively and feel more restored. Attention restoration theory (ART) states that time in natural spaces can replenish our ability to manage our attention, concentrate, and be mindfully present in our daily lives and in our holiday gatherings — and in the process help prevent feelings of loneliness and isolation.

The American Psychological Association has stated that the healing and therapeutic benefits of spending time in natural spaces are available even after only spending two hours each week in nature. By setting aside less than 30 minutes a day to walk, unplug, breathe deeply, and mindfully take in our surroundings, we can begin to experience the restorative energy that nature has to offer. Even limited exposure to nature can be beneficial. Simply viewing nature can have a calming and positive influence on both physical and emotional well-being (Tahmaseb McConatha et al., 2023).

As the holidays approach, one way to stay grounded and prevent burnout is to reconnect with natural spaces. One simple practice is to listen to the trees. This experience can be deepened by finding a comfortable place near or beneath a tree and sitting quietly for a few moments. Even five minutes can help calm the mind and body.

There is no need to find the perfect spot or the perfect tree, or to set expectations or goals for your practice. Instead, give yourself permission to pause, be present, and take in the world around you. Simply engage your senses by noticing the sounds, scents, colors, textures, and gentle movements of nature. Allow yourself to become more aware of your surroundings and embrace the quiet of the moment.

When you are ready to move on, thank your tree for being there and offering stillness, comfort, and a place to simply be.

Renewing transcendence can be a regular practice. It does not require anything other than slowing down, connecting with nature and senses, and allowing ourselves to be fully present.

Fromm, E. (1973). The Anatomy of Human Destructiveness. New York: Holt, Rinehart and Winston.

Kaplan, R., & Kaplan, S. (1989). The experience of nature: A psychological perspective. Cambridge University Press.

McConatha JT, Ford K, Cusmano C, Lyman N, McConatha M. (2023) The Healing Power of Green Spaces: Combating Loneliness, Loss, and Isolation. International Journal of Geriatrics and Gerontology, 7(176). https://doi.org/10.29011/2577-0748.100076

Tornstam, L. (1997). Gerotranscendence: The contemplative dimension of aging. Journal of Aging Studies,11(2), 143–154. 10.1016/S0890-4065(97)90018-9

Wilson, E. O. (1984). Biophilia, Harvard University Press.

#4764. Everyone wants an electric pickup truck. I want more electric 125cc motorcycles

If you follow the EV industry in North America, you’d be forgiven for thinking that the future of transportation revolves around electric SUVs and pickups. Every week seems to bring another teaser from a startup promising to reinvent the family car or truck. The latest electric SUVs, “coming soon” tiny trucks, lifestyle trucks, modular trucks, etc. Companies like Slate, TELO, and countless others have generated plenty of excitement, even if many of them still have everything left to prove.

Don’t get me wrong – I hope they succeed. We need more affordable electric vehicles. But after spending nearly two decades covering a specific part of the electric-vehicle space and a good chunk of that time traveling around the world to see how people actually get around, I can’t help but wonder if we’re chasing the wrong prize here.

Because while the West keeps trying to electrify pickup trucks and SUVs, much of the world has already settled on a far more sensible transportation appliance.

Western readers often think of a sedan as the world’s “normal” or “sensible” vehicle.

But go traveling almost anywhere in Asia, and that illusion disappears in about five minutes.

The roads are filled with Honda Clicks and CG125s, Hero Splendors, Yamaha NMAXs and YBR125s, and countless other small-displacement motorcycles. They carry workers to jobs, students to school, families to dinner, and every imaginable cargo in between.

They’re the delivery vans. They’re the commuter cars. They’re grocery getters, family transportation, and work trucks. And perhaps more importantly, they transport hundreds of millions of people every single day.

You don’t have to spend long in places like the Philippines before realizing something else: these aren’t really “motorcycle cultures.” They’re just transportation cultures. People ride these machines because they make sense.

And I’ve done it myself to see what all the fuss was about. Sure, I’m an e-motorcycle guy through and through. But I’ve been there to ride a mile in their motorcycle sandals, and so I get it.

Even so, having had one cheek on each saddle, I still have to think there’s a better way than the tried-and-true 125cc combustion engine motorcycles that have become the workhorse of much of the world.

The extreme proliferation of small motorcycles is what makes the current electric motorcycle market feel so strange. If there were ever a class of gasoline vehicle that batteries are already capable of replacing, it’s the 125cc combustion engine motorcycle.

These bikes aren’t demanding. They generally produce a modest 10-15 hp (8–11 kW) of power. They cruise comfortably around 45-60 mph (70-100 km/h). Most riders travel relatively short daily distances measured in dozens of miles, not hundreds.

A modern electric motorcycle with a 4-6 kWh battery can comfortably accomplish those same tasks while offering smoother acceleration, quieter operation, lower maintenance, and dramatically lower operating costs.

Unlike replacing a heavy-duty pickup truck that tows livestock trailers across Montana, replacing a 125cc commuter bike is already well within today’s battery technology. In many ways, it’s one of the easiest transportation sectors to electrify.

Instead, North America’s electric motorcycle market developed in an odd direction.

We have electric bicycles, and those are great for urban commuters. But then we jump almost straight to premium electric motorcycles costing $15,000 to $25,000. The practical middle has remained surprisingly sparse.

The ONYX RCR became something of a cult favorite by proving there was genuine demand for lightweight, motorcycle-like electric transportation without superbike performance.

Ryvid’s Anthem pushed further, adding highway capability while still remaining approachable and relatively affordable.

The new LiveWire S4 Honcho also feels like an encouraging step toward a lighter, more practical electric motorcycle instead of another oversized premium machine.

Even Infinite Machine’s Olto, while occupying a slightly different category, demonstrates growing interest in practical urban electric two-wheelers that prioritize transportation over headline horsepower.

These companies are proving something important: People don’t necessarily need 100 horsepower. Many simply need transportation.

Don’t misunderstand me. Electric pickup trucks absolutely have their place. Electric SUVs do too.

But we’ve spent the last decade pouring enormous engineering effort into electrifying some of the least energy-efficient passenger vehicles on the road.

Meanwhile, we’ve largely ignored one of the most efficient gasoline vehicle classes humanity has ever created.

A typical 125cc combustion engine motorcycle can already achieve fuel economy approaching or exceeding 100 mpg (2.35 liters/100 km). An electric equivalent becomes almost absurdly efficient.

We’re talking roughly 4-6 kWh per 100 kilometers (62 miles) – just a fraction of the energy consumed even by many compact electric cars. I once did the math, and a light electric motorcycle can travel 10,000 km (roughly 6,000 miles) for around $160 in electricity. Basically, your electrical bill doesn’t even notice when you own an electric motorcycle. Charging it simply doesn’t move the needle.

Instead of asking how we can fit ever-larger battery packs into increasingly larger SUVs and trucks, perhaps we should also be asking how many trips don’t need a large vehicle in the first place.

Transportation statistics across much of the developed world tell a familiar story.

Most trips involve one person. Maybe there’s also a backpack in the mix. Maybe there are some groceries getting picked up on the way home. Occasionally, there’s another passenger.

Those things are exactly what small motorcycles have been doing around the world for decades.

I recently spent some time in the Philippines, where I watched motorcycles carrying impossible-looking loads every day. Entire families would ride together. Construction materials. Furniture. Livestock. I saw two pigs on a 125cc bike, I kid you not. I’ve seen even crazier things in Thailand.

Again, I’m certainly not advocating that we adopt some of those practices in the West – there are obvious safety considerations – but it demonstrates just how incredibly capable these machines can be.

Even within normal Western expectations, a 125cc-class motorcycle is capable of handling an astonishing percentage of daily transportation needs.

This is where discussions about motorcycles often become unnecessarily polarized.

No, motorcycles aren’t ideal in every situation. Yes, heavy rain exists. Snow exists. Families with multiple children exist. Long interstate road trips exist.

Nobody is suggesting a 125cc electric motorcycle should replace every car.

If a household can replace even half of its daily driving with a lightweight electric motorcycle, that’s already a massive reduction in energy consumption, congestion, parking demand, and transportation costs.

Transportation doesn’t have to be all-or-nothing. So enough with this “but what if it rains?” stuff. Either put on a jacket that day or drive your car. But for the majority of the trips each year you take where it’s not raining, you could have done it in a much more efficient (and fun) way.

One of the biggest conversations surrounding EV adoption is charging. But smaller electric motorcycles barely participate in that problem. A 4-5 kWh battery charges overnight from an ordinary household outlet. The outlet you plug your laptop charger into is basically the equivalent of a Level 2 public charger for an e-motorcycle – that’s how fast it is.

DC fast charging isn’t really necessary on a light electric motorcycle. There’s no need for an expensive home charger. There’s no massive battery pack. Just plug it in before bed and wake up with a battery that’s been fully charged and waiting on you for hours already.

And if you want to go wild, there are swappable battery networks like Gogoro in Taiwan or Vammo in South America that can make charging unnecessary.

Another advantage rarely discussed is intimidation. Many people don’t want a 600 lb (270 kg) motorcycle producing superbike acceleration. They want something approachable, something lightweight, maneuverable, easy to park, and easy to live with.

That’s exactly why 125cc motorcycles became so successful globally.

Electric versions preserve all of those advantages while making them even easier to ride thanks to instant torque and the absence of clutch work. Many of them even come with reverse mode, making them easier to park and wiggle around even on hilly terrain.

One reason Europe has seen more progress here is that the regulatory framework already exists.

Manufacturers regularly market bikes as “125cc equivalents,” and consumers immediately understand what that means.

Licensing systems and insurance companies recognize the category. It’s a mature transportation class.

North America, by comparison, often treats motorcycles as either recreational toys or large-displacement touring machines. We’ve largely forgotten that much of the world simply sees them as transportation.

Ironically, younger riders may already be showing us the way forward.

The explosion in popularity of Sur Ron-style electric motorcycles and lightweight e-motos demonstrates that younger generations are perfectly willing to embrace two-wheeled electric transportation.

Not everyone buying those bikes is looking for motocross. Many simply enjoy the freedom, accessibility, affordability, and fun that come with traveling on two wheels.

Rather than dismissing that trend, perhaps we should recognize it as an opportunity. Today’s recreational rider often becomes tomorrow’s commuter.

If someone discovers they enjoy getting around on an electric two-wheeler, moving from a lightweight e-moto to a practical 125cc-equivalent commuter becomes a much smaller leap than convincing someone to abandon their car entirely.

One observation has stuck with me after so many years of covering the electric vehicle industry and traveling through countries where motorcycles dominate daily life. The West has spent years trying to electrify the largest, heaviest, and least efficient vehicles on our roads. Meanwhile, we’ve paid surprisingly little attention to electrifying the vehicle that already moves much of humanity every single day.

In Europe at least, there's a cliff between a pedal ebike, which anyone can ride without any pre planning, and a motorcycle which needs passing a specific test, taxing, taking out insurance and wearing safety gear. Even people with car licences need to take driving lessons and the test. It means you can't just step on a motorcycle when it makes sense you need potentially months of planning. It's much easier just to take a car you're already licensed for.

I’m not arguing that everyone should ride a motorcycle. And I’m certainly not arguing that cars no longer have an important place.

But perhaps we’ve underestimated just how many people could benefit from something in between.

Not just an electric bicycle, and not just a $25,000 electric motorcycle. Just an honest, practical, affordable electric equivalent of the vehicle that already keeps much of the world moving.

Because if we’re serious about accelerating electric transportation, maybe the future isn’t another electric pickup truck. Maybe it’s finally giving the world’s favorite motorcycle an electric motor.

#4762. RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” said Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

“The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse said.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

“There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.

#4760. Did a Narcissistic Boss Cost You Your Career?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Prada was a 29-year-old registered nurse when she came to my office in tears, saying she hated her job and was having panic attacks. Sharon, the hospital’s human resources director, perceived that the trauma exposure in her work in the emergency room was the source of the panic attacks and sent her to specialized resilience training.

Devin, a 42-year-old software architect, came to my office with concerns about depression. He feared losing his job because he was too old and believed that new artificial intelligence programs were replacing him.

At first glance, their struggles seemed understandable, given the unique demands of their professions. The trauma exposure, aging concerns, and technological pressures were real. But more conversations revealed something deeper and more destabilizing: a high-achieving, abusive, and narcissistic boss.

The challenge is that organizations often view a high-achiever as the goose that lays the golden egg, making them revered and supported. But when that high-achiever also commits narcissistic abuse, they can be untouchable. And the fallout of their abusive tactics resides in the long-term wounds of countless victims.

In It's Not You: Identifying and Healing from Narcissistic People, Ramani Durvasula describes how many therapists are trained to address the person’s isolated symptoms and often miss the larger impacts of narcissistic relationships. She also echoes what Lundy Bancroft explained almost 25 years ago in Why Does He Do That? Inside the Minds of Angry and Controlling Men—the abusive person is a master of disguise and actually gains footing with the therapist, while the abused person who shows up as anxious and closed can get further gaslit and retraumatized by the therapist. Moreover, interventions focused on appeasement or better communication can reinforce and escalate manipulation and abusive tactics.

Now imagine that third party is HR, an executive coach, or an organizational consultant.

And imagine that the abusive person is exceptionally accomplished, charismatic, influential, and valuable to the organization.

Who gets believed? Who gets coached? Who gets labeled difficult? And who quietly disappears from the organization?

Given these complex dynamics, I was surprised to read an article in the Journal of Business Ethics suggesting that clear codes of conduct and consequences could help address narcissistically abusive supervision. The authors’ research revealed that leaders high in narcissistic rivalry employ abusive supervision when they perceive employees as deviating from their authority or organizational rules; yet they suggest: “It is essential that organizations recognize the importance of fostering a supportive environment in which both leaders and followers are equipped with the skills and knowledge to interact respectfully with each other” (Gauglitz & Schyns, 2024).

While rules for conduct can establish best practices and delineate what is prohibited, they may fail to address the hidden dynamics of manipulation, coercion, and stealth sabotage.

In Ten Keys to Staying Empowered in a Power Struggle, I explain how manipulative tactics often operate through confusing double-binds, intermittent praise, shifting expectations, selective memory, and gaslighting. These patterns can leave people questioning their judgment while the person causing harm appears credible and composed.

I have witnessed people who left jobs—and entire careers—without understanding how an abusive workplace dynamic eroded their confidence, health, and sense of agency.

If something like this happened to you, or someone you know, consider these five questions:

In contrast, healthy workplace dynamics and leadership allow disagreement without humiliation, accountability without retaliation, and growth without diminishing someone's dignity.

Sometimes, recognizing what happened is the first step toward healing, which involves reclaiming what you lost, honoring what you endured, and breaking the cycle of abuse that continues long after the abuser is gone through self-blame, shame, and the transformation of someone else’s cruelty into your own inner voice.

Gauglitz, I. K., & Schyns, B. (20240801). Triggered Abuse: How and Why Leaders with Narcissistic Rivalry React to Follower Deviance. Journal of Business Ethics, 193(1), 115–131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10551-023-05579-7

#4758. New ID. AURA is the mainstream EV VW needs – but its software is the real story

Volkswagen built its global empire on the promise of affordable, accessible transportation, embodied by the iconic Type 1 Beetle. Now facing an existential crisis after a decades-long push upmarket, the automaker faces a reckoning – and a retreat back into affordable, mass-market electric sedans like the new FAW-VW ID. AURA L5 (and the software that powers it) might be exactly what VW needs to reach a new generation of buyers.

Like the Ford Model T, the original VW Type 1 Beetle was an engineering-led answer to a basic problem: making family transportation affordable and accessible to the masses. And regardless of how you feel about Elon Musk, the Tesla Model 3 has become the spiritual successor to those cars, bringing electric transportation to millions of mainstream drivers. As the Model 3 approaches its 11th year in public view, the recently revealed all-electric ID. AURA L5 and VW JETTA looks like it could be a compelling rival to the mainstream M3.

Co-developed by Volkswagen’s Chinese and German design teams and set to be built by the FAW-VW JV, the ID. AURA L5 is an Accord/Camry-sized electric family car a practical fastback-style rear hatch, frameless doors, and a claimed “84.4% usable floor-area ratio.” The power-operated hatchback opens its maw more than 70 degrees, revealing a 39″ wide opening that can handle groceries, luggage, golf clubs, pets, bodies – whatever you got.

Don’t take my word for it, though. This is the original text from the company’s press release (translated from Chinese by Google):

The ID. AURA L5 is a pure electric family sedan, jointly designed by Chinese and German design teams, and highly replicates the design essence of the ID. AURA concept car shown at the 2025 Shanghai Auto Show. Its short overhang and long wheelbase proportions create a sleek and flowing coupe-like stance, achieving a “usable floor area ratio” of 84.4%. The sides feature true frameless doors, semi-concealed door handles, and an electric hatchback tailgate with an opening angle exceeding 70°, and an opening width exceeding 1000 mm, greatly improving the convenience of loading and unloading large items, deeply integrating fastback aesthetics with practicality. Some models will be equipped with LiDAR and feature the Hyper Sense 8 end-to-end large model, making daily travel easier and more convenient for customers.

The production version of the ID. AURA L5 is expected to pack the same 155 kW (~208 hp) electric motors announced when the concept AURA L5 was first shown last year (battery specs were not released), and was shown as part of a broader product announcement of what VW Group China would be showcasing at this year’s China International Import Expo (CIIE). These include the first two models fully equipped with Volkswagen Group’s locally developed VEGA “integrated technology matrix” (read: software), and the Volkswagen Anhui intelligent pure electric “coupe” crossover.

The announcement coincides with reports from outlets like Autocar and Reuters that Volkswagen is evaluating whether to deploy its China-developed electrical architecture across the majority of its European markets.

“According to internal discussions confirmed by Group board member and Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer,” reports Autocar’s Greg Kable, “up to 75% of the firm’s core models in Europe could eventually use the China Electronic Architecture.”

The Volkswagen Group has been struggling to deliver a software experience that resonates with customers. To their credit, they’re looking for outside help, spending billions of dollars on a software collaboration with EV startup Rivian for its upcoming electric truck brand Scout rather than going it alone. With billions of dollars and potential future of the company at stake, then, this seems like the most interesting bit of the announcement:

During the event, the immersive interactive experience exhibit “Digital Magic Cube,” which made its debut at last year’s China International Import Expo, will undergo an iterative upgrade to showcase the core strength of CEA (China Electronic Architecture), the software pillar of Volkswagen Group’s integrated self-developed technology matrix VEGA, to the attendees.

To date, CEA has enabled five new models from three joint ventures within the Volkswagen Group on a large scale, and software iterations have already been completed this year. CEA brings three core advantages to the Group’s new model lineup in China: intelligent accessibility, continuous upgrades, and safety redundancy. Through immersive interactive presentations, it provides consumers with the most intuitive experience. Empowered by the new AI R&D toolchain “C-Brain,” CEA introduces AI agents into software development, design, and engineering verification, enabling more flexible and efficient integration and innovation of vehicle intelligence capabilities, giving vehicles powerful thinking and perception abilities. Intelligent vehicles powered by CEA can better understand consumer needs, more efficiently create in-vehicle intelligent application scenarios, and better enhance digital intelligent safety redundancy, bringing Chinese consumers a new generation of intelligent mobility experience defined by Volkswagen standards

Sensible looking average car which should appeal to VW buyers provided the price, charging speed and range are right. Especially like that it has a hatch without being SUV shaped.

The show runs through November 10th, and we’ll be keeping an eye out for more details on the ID. AURA lineup and the Anhui intelligent pure electric coupe, including its powertrain, battery, and software specifications, as they become available.

#4757. This bear’s big butt is so beautiful, it just won an award

Published Nov 10, 2026 3:13 PM EST

Yes, bears are big. Depending on the time of year and sex, the average black bear (Ursus americanus) weighs between 90 to 500 pounds. On average brown bears (Ursus arctos) can weigh between 600 to 900 pounds. However, one female black bear named Volverine is a true fat bear queen this year. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded her with the 2026 Big & Beautiful Award for her heft.

The rangers say that this mother bear is a “true icon,” who will often pose on a rock for a long time, seemingly allowing the visitors to Anan Wildlife Observatory to take photos. She is regarded as one of the most beautiful bears at Anan, with a chest patch shaped like the letter V. Volverine is also on the bigger end of the black bear spectrum, with a potato-shaped body, and an especially round butt. Her fishing skills made her one of the largest bears of the 2026 season—and a dominant matriarch.

“Our rangers love to see a fat female bear because that could mean cubs next year!” the rangers write. “Bears have what’s called delayed implantation, meaning they mate in the spring, and IF they get fat enough, the embryos implant in the fall.”

Wishing Volverine and all of the bears the best this winter season.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. The run is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Like their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks. Volverine would fit right in with Katmai’s chunky brown bears, despite the fact that black bears tend to be a bit smaller.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of what they are up to 24/7.

#4756. When Your Cofounder Isn’t Who You Vetted

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

You’re driving home from the pitch, replaying the way your cofounder talked over you in front of the investor. The part that stings is that you did this carefully. You went through the cofounder dating questions together. You spent more time vetting them than most other founders you know. But you still ended up frustrated and disappointed, thinking to yourself: How did I choose wrong?

Most founders I work with put time and energy into selecting their cofounder. Many used Gloria Lin’s 50 questions, published by First Round Review. These questions are useful, but the problem is often that the answers were true when you gave them, and people change, especially under pressure.

Two founders I worked with demonstrated this clearly.

One of them was leaving an established company to start the business. Sarah was worried about what failing would do to her reputation and felt concerned she couldn't simply re-enter her role if she left. So she set a condition. She'd only make the leap if her partner, Tom, was willing to give up everything for the company: his sleep, his health, his marriage. Tom said yes, and he meant it (at the time).

Then Tom's wife got very sick. His priorities shifted, and he no longer wanted to prioritize the company above his marriage. He worked fewer hours. Sarah saw that as a breach of contract. Tom hoped that Sarah would change her mind and the two of them could keep building. But Sarah wasn’t willing to budge. She was quite clear on the level of sacrifice and commitment to the business she required, and they ultimately parted ways.

Looking back, the warning signs were present in their first conversation.

Sarah's demand was extreme. It highlighted unconscious anxiety about her inability to recover the prestige of her previous company and corresponding rigidity about sacrifice and commitment. The partnership agreement was also too inflexible. When Tom's life changed, they didn't have the capacity to change the terms.

I find it useful to separate aspirational values from lived values. Aspirational values are the ones you’d list if someone asked you. Lived values are what someone watching your behavior would see.

When cofounders answer each other’s questions before they start, they’re mostly reporting aspirational values. They mean them. They just haven’t had to live them yet.

A core idea in psychoanalysis is that we’re of many minds, and that the conscious mind doesn’t always win.

Partnerships within a startup environment prove that point. Founders are often exhausted, sick, and under pressure, and in my experience, people regress under that kind of load. They fall back on older, less flexible ways of coping. It’s easy to say you’ll stay calm in a disagreement. It’s much harder when your heart is pounding, your revenue isn't growing, and you’re frustrated with the person across the table.

In a 1995 review in Psychological Bulletin, the psychologists Benjamin Karney and Thomas Bradbury drew on 115 longitudinal studies covering more than 45,000 marriages and proposed what they called the vulnerability-stress-adaptation model.

In their model, how a marriage fares depends on three things working together: what each partner brings into the relationship, such as personality and family history; the stress the couple faces; and how the two of them treat each other under that stress.

A couple can look steady when life is calm and struggle once the pressure rises. I see the same thing with cofounders, and a startup supplies plenty of pressure.

Two other cofounders I worked with had been colleagues at a previous company. Before starting, they agreed to a chart spelling out who was responsible for each area and who would be consulted or just informed on each decision.

The technical cofounder signed off on being informed about areas outside his own. What he actually expected was to be consulted, because to him that’s what being a cofounder meant. His partner saw the cofounder title as little more than extra equity. What mattered to her was running separate areas and moving fast. Nobody asked what “informed” meant, and the mismatch only surfaced once they were building.

Gaps like this tend to get pushed aside, because they feel less urgent than shipping a product or landing customers. Founders tell themselves they’ll talk once the demo works, then once they have more customers.

In my experience, the company usually grows faster than the partnership does. Whatever got skipped early comes back later, often at a bad moment, like the middle of a fundraise, when you’re also deciding who’ll be the face of the company to investors.

The questions are a starting point. The test is working together long enough, ideally several months, to say yes to two things: We’re aligned on what we’re building, and I know how you act under stress. It helps to think in milestones rather than a set number of weeks.

The first yes covers the practical side: where you want the business to go, how you’ll fund it, what financial outcome each of you wants, how much risk each of you is taking on, and how much time and sacrifice each of you can give.

The second yes is about the two of you. Have you seen how your partner responds when things get hard, and do you still enjoy working with them? Can you give each other feedback in both directions? Have you had a genuine disagreement and come back from it?

That last one carries a lot of weight. In my work, trust between partners tends to grow through repeated cycles of rupture and repair, and the honeymoon period doesn’t offer many of those.

Before you sign anything, agree on how you’ll adjust equity, compensation, or roles if that were needed, and write it down. Most people’s life circumstances and values change at some point. What hurt the founders in my story was having no agreed way to adjust when that happened.

If you are successful, you'll spend the next 5 to 10 years with this person. Building resilience in a relationship requires going through hardship together and coming through aligned on the other side. There's no question that can preempt that.

Karney, B. R., & Bradbury, T. N. (1995). The longitudinal course of marital quality and stability: A review of theory, method, and research. Psychological Bulletin, 118(1), 3–34. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.118.1.3

#4755. French carmaker Renault wants to get into the military robot business

Forget what your Fox News-addicted uncle told you about cheese-eating surrender monkeys. The French military has centuries of storied military victories and traditions behind it, and Renault wants in on that action with a new, autonomous electric vehicle platform designed to tackle the Armée de Terre’s most demanding missions.

Co-developed by the EV experts at Renault Group and the defense experts at Belgian electronics firm John Cockerill, the new Forefront concept previews a new, modular ground vehicle that can be rapidly industrialized at a controlled cost, with unique mobility and off-road performance, and capable of autonomously navigating complex terrain. The result is a machine that could front-line logistical capabilities for both defense and civilian applications, enabling missions to be carried out remotely in very high-risk and hard‑to‑reach environments.

“Forefront Concept … demonstrates the contribution that Renault Group’s industrial and technological expertise can make to a strategic sector such as unmanned ground vehicles with multiple applications expected across both civilian and military sectors in the years to come,” explains François Provost, CEO, Renault Group. “This innovative project brings together two complementary areas of expertise: Renault Group’s in the rapid, large-scale and cost-effective development and production of high-performance, reliable technological products and John Cockerill’s in the defense industry.”

Renault is quick to point out that its new concept isn’t just suitable for military work. Although it’s worth pointing out that the Renault-provided image, above, isn’t just AI slop: it would be impractical if it was real, with no real obvious way to get those RCP pipes on or off the thing. That said, presenting their military killbot as a construction mule is at least more credible than the “ambulance” and “troop transport” use cases we’ve seen touted by similar concepts on the American side.

Call me cynical but military contracts are the best and last refuge for a company that cannot compete in the open market. With no / limited international competition, a famously slow procurement process that favors "proven" (read 3+ generation old) technology, and equipment that is rarely used in a competitive environment and whose failures are cloaked behind national security classifications, it is the perfect place to hide. (C.f. Oshkosh and AM General)

Forefront seems to be little more than a rendering at this stage, with the first of the Forefront concept prototypes set to take part in a number of exercises and trials in the months ahead to further refine the concept.

#4754. Why Living with Endometriosis May Double Your Odds of Migraine

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich said endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

#4753. College student develops LEGO-like, 3D-printed moon bricks

Published Nov 10, 2026 4:30 PM EST

A permanent lunar base will require structures resilient enough to withstand everything from cosmic radiation and micro-meteorites to moonquakes. There are plenty of building materials to choose from on Earth, but they all come with a catch: transportation storage aboard spacecraft is limited, and each additional pound of cargo will quickly ramp up costs. Engineers have spent years experimenting with ways for future astronauts to source local lunar ingredients, including fine moon dust known as regolith. Unfortunately, most require various binding ingredients that must still be sent from back home.

A college student at the University of Arkansas (U of A) recently had a different idea. In a collaboration with U of A mechanical engineer Wan Shou, Cole McCallum harnessed a specialized method of 3D printing to manufacture LEGO-esque bricks from lunar dust, no binding required. (These aren’t to be confused with LEGO’s actual lunar bricks mockups). Their results published in the journal NPJ Advanced Manufacturing indicate the bricks could be a promising material to investigate as humanity readies itself for a return to the moon.

Lunar regolith is a tricky material. Unlike Earth’s dirt, it doesn’t contain any amount of organic matter. It’s just loose, sharp-edged particles generated by billions’ of years of asteroid and meteor impacts. This means that moon dust can’t bind on its own and requires at least some secondary ingredients.

While an undergraduate at the U of A, McCallum wondered if a specific type of 3D printing called laser powder bed fusion could offer a workaround. In this technique, fine powder is placed on a flat bed, then exposed to a highly powerful laser beam that fuses each microscopic particle together in a process called sintering. The tray bed lowers down to allow another layer of sintered powder, then repeats the steps until a single, solid block is created. Regolith fits the mold perfectly, so to speak.

“There’s nothing else it’s binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself,” McCallum said in a university profile.

McCallum and Shou didn’t have access to actual lunar material, so they obtained Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1), a commercial material that replicates the moon dust collected by Apollo astronauts during the 1960s and 70s. They ultimately settled on two shapes, one that resembles a cross and another that looks like the letter “H.” The researchers then 3D-printed tiny prototypes measuring a few centimeters wide that they could connect like LEGOs to construct larger structures.

There are still some important caveats to this sintered regolith strategy. McCallum’s blocks are much more porous and weaker than materials containing binders. Additional research is needed to see how the approach works in a vacuum or microgravity, two inescapable hurdles to living on the moon.

“These structures we’re making can be self-supported. But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that’s supporting other loads at this moment yet,” said McCallum.

That said, his demonstration that even a basic framework for lunar base bricks is achievable solely with regolith may offer a promising direction for mission engineers

#4752. 'Not High, Not Drunk, Just Hungry'

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Just beyond the bridge, there’s a man in the middle of the roadway. He’s standing there on the thin divide between coming and going, speeding up to make the light and slowing down when it turns red, entering the city and getting out of town.

My daughter and I are leaving. The sun is sinking on another long day of work and school. If only my car could fly like the Jetsons’, we’d be home instead of inching along in this clogged line where the drivers’ aggravations rise like exhaust fumes into the twilight.

As we edge closer to the man, it’s the sign that grabs my attention. Simple. Clever. To the point.

That’s what it says as he waits, message in one hand, and a Whole Foods shopping bag in the other. Standing there on the thin divide between a warm car and a cold street, a full tank and an empty stomach, a way out and no way out.

If traffic were moving, I could just drive by. I wouldn’t have to look. I wouldn’t have to think. Stuck here in this jam, it’s not that easy.

He knows this. He’s smart. His little roadside marketing campaign has all the right elements. Know your audience. Address their concerns. Eliminate their objections. Appeal to their needs. Basic human needs. Food, water, that sort of thing.

The Whole Foods bag is a nice touch. Without a word, he’s telling us his intentions are good. Organic, pure and wholesome. And to think we might have suspected otherwise.

Motor running. Car stalled. Mind racing. Time suspended. I reach for my purse.

“Mom, you’re not going to give him money?”

My daughter’s words, yes. But they come from me, from what I’ve taught her over the years. Don’t talk to strangers. Don’t stop. Don’t get involved. You never really know who they are. You never really know where they come from. You never really know what they’re doing there in the middle of the roadway.

Especially now. In these hard times when the rules have all changed.

I roll down my window. The wind whips against my face as I hand the man a few crumpled bills I might have used for a cappuccino. He smiles. I search his eyes for something. Reassurance? About him? About me? The light turns green. We drive away.

But in my rearview mirror, I catch a glimpse of him alongside another car, another rolled-down window, another arm extended into the night.

Standing there on the thin divide between doubt and faith, cynicism and optimism, despair and hope.
